1.text: WORK IN STONE. — Stone tools and weapons are no longer used in

2.text: northeastern Asia by the men. The more conservative women have preserved

3.text: some of the implements, and even sought to increase their importance by

4.text: connecting them with religious ceremonies. This was the case with the kitchen

6.text: In the remotest parts of the country, — for example, among the Kerek, —

7.text: stone adzes and knives were discarded within the remembrance of the living

8.text: generation, not more than fifteen or twenty years ago, according to statements

9.text: of older people made to me in villages of that tribe.

10.text: Among the Chukchee and the Asiatic Eskimo stone implements of this

11.text: class disappeared more than half a century ago. Their character can be

12.text: ascertained only from specimens found in old houses and on burial-places.

13.text: By comparing these implements with those found in other parts of north-

14.text: eastern Asia, it seems that the harpoon-heads, spears, and arrows of the

15.text: whole region were usually made of flint, slate, obsidian, and sometimes of

16.text: quartz. The pieces of obsidian occasionally found in the country at the present

17.text: time are regarded as lightning arrows and balls which from time to time

18.text: drop from the sky. The arrow-points made of obsidian are generally ruder

19.text: than those made of flint. By carefully chipping off thin pieces the natives

20.text: seem to have often made the flint arrow-heads with quite symmetrical outlines

22.text: The slate implements were flat, and had their edges rubbed down with

23.text: another stone. To assist in fastening these to the shaft, the Chukchee made

24.text: holes in the slate, using a slender drill, and working alternately on opposite

25.text: sides until the blade was pierced. One of the slate specimens in the Museum

26.text: has a circular mark on each side, showing how they had started to drill holes.

27.text: The slate blades were rather weak and ineffectual. I was told by the

28.text: older people that a fresh blade was usually placed in the whaling-harpoon

29.text: after each blow, on account of the old one being spoiled. Slate was more

30.text: appropriate for knives, and fragments of these are found in almost every old

31.text: “jaw-bone” house. Regarding stone implements used at present in woman’s

33.text: Bone, ivory, and antler were used also for all kinds of weapons, such as

34.text: harpoons, arrows, etc. After the appearance of iron, they held their ground

35.text: much better than the stone tools. Of the specimens found in old Chukchee

36.text: and Eskimo houses, only a few bear traces of having been made with stone
